title: Presentation Architecture: MVC, MVP, MVVM, MVI
scopeHtml: Scope: why architecture exists on Android, how MVC/MVP/MVVM/MVI differ and evolved, Google's layered guidance, state holder vs presenter, testability and lifecycle, reducers, Redux-style libraries, and choosing by team and screen complexity. UDF state modeling, one-off events and ViewModel internals live in other chunks (U1, E1, V1).

questions.promptHtml: Why do we need an app architecture on Android at all? Can't we just write the logic in the Activity and ship?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They want to see whether you understand that Android architecture is driven by platform constraints (lifecycle, process death), not by fashion.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "You can ship that way, but it stops scaling quickly. The Activity is owned by the OS: it is destroyed on rotation, on low memory, and the process can be killed. So data, business logic and networking in it get lost or tangled, and nothing is testable without an emulator. Architecture is separation of concerns: UI renders state, a state holder owns screen logic, a data layer owns data. That gives me survival across config changes, unit-testable logic, and several engineers working without merge conflicts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
First principles: Android components (Activity, Service, Receiver) can be launched individually, out of order, and destroyed at any time. Google's guidance says do not store app data or state in app components. A 1,500-line MainActivity that does HttpURLConnection calls, parses JSON and mutates views has three problems:

  1. Lifecycle coupling. Rotation recreates the Activity, so in-flight requests either leak the old Activity or are re-fired.
  2. No seams. You cannot run it on the JVM, so tests need an emulator (minutes per run, flaky).
  3. No ownership. Every feature touches the same file, so merge conflicts and unclear responsibility.

Architecture gives you boundaries:

UI elements (Compose / Views)  -> render state, forward events
State holder (ViewModel)       -> screen logic, exposes immutable state
Data layer (repositories)      -> source of truth, business rules, threading

The point is not the pattern name. Each boundary buys one concrete thing: the state holder buys config-change survival and JVM testability; the repository buys a single source of truth and swappable sources.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: logic, state and IO in the Activity
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    private var items: List<Item> = emptyList() // lost on rotation
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        thread { items = api.loadItems(); runOnUiThread { render() } } // leaks Activity, refires on rotate
    }
}

// Better: Activity only renders
class ItemsViewModel(private val repo: ItemsRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val uiState: StateFlow<ItemsUiState> = repo.items
        .map { ItemsUiState.Success(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ItemsUiState.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "for testability" without naming what is untestable (anything needing Context, lifecycle, or main looper).
  • Treating architecture as mandatory ceremony; a 3-screen utility can be simple (see Q020).
  • Believing ViewModel solves process death. It survives configuration change only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What exactly survives rotation and what does not? → ViewModel instances and their in-memory state survive a config change; Activity and view state do not, and none of it survives process death unless saved (SavedStateHandle/persistence).
  2. Where does the pattern name matter? → It matters less than the rules: who owns state, which direction data flows, who may reference whom.
  3. What is the cost of architecture? → Indirection, more files, onboarding; justified when team size, screen count or test needs justify it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "to separate concerns and make code testable." Senior: ties each layer to a failure mode (lifecycle, process death, merge contention), and names what it costs and when to stop.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Typical legacy rescue: a checkout Activity fired the payment request in onCreate; rotation during payment produced duplicate calls. Moving the call into a state holder that outlives the Activity fixed it.

questions.promptHtml: What is MVC, and why does it map badly onto classic Android with Activities and XML layouts?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the baseline to evaluate whether you understand what MVP and MVVM were reacting to.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "MVC splits Model (data and rules), View (rendering) and Controller (input handling, updating the model). On classic Android the XML is the view, but the Activity ends up being both controller and view: it inflates views, handles clicks, calls the model, and updates widgets. So the 'controller' is welded to a lifecycle-bound framework class, becomes huge, and can't be unit tested. That is why people moved to MVP and then MVVM."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In textbook MVC the View observes the Model and the Controller is a separate object. On Android:

XML layout (View, dumb)  <---- findViewById / setText ---- Activity
                                                          (View + Controller)
                                                               |
                                                            Model (POJOs, DB, network)

The Activity must touch widgets (TextView.setText), so it is the view in practice. It also receives lifecycle callbacks, onActivityResult, permissions and clicks, so it is also the controller. Result: "Massive View Controller" (the same disease exists on iOS). Consequences: logic cannot run on the JVM (needs Robolectric or instrumentation), and recreation on rotation re-runs everything.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContentView(R.layout.activity_profile)
        findViewById<Button>(R.id.save).setOnClickListener {
            val name = findViewById<EditText>(R.id.name).text.toString()
            if (name.isBlank()) { /* validation in the view class */ return@setOnClickListener }
            api.save(name) // IO + threading + view updates all here
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming Android "has no MVC". It has the shape of one, with a conflated View/Controller.
  • Blaming XML. The problem is where the logic lives, not the markup.
  • Equating the model with "the database". The model includes rules and state.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Compose MVC? → No class named controller; composables render state, events go up via lambdas to a state holder. Closer to UDF/MVVM/MVI.
  2. Why did Fragments not fix it? → They are the same problem with a more complex lifecycle (view lifecycle vs fragment lifecycle).
  3. What did MVP change structurally? → It extracted the logic out of the framework class behind an interface (Q003).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Activity is both view and controller." Senior: explains the consequence in test seams and lifecycle, and notes that evolution to MVP/MVVM is about moving logic off framework classes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Legacy modules with 3k-line Activities are where crash-rate regressions cluster, because every change touches state, IO and UI in one scope.

questions.promptHtml: Explain MVP on Android. What is a contract, what is a passive view, and what problem did it solve?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many large codebases still run MVP; you need to read and migrate it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "In MVP the View is an interface implemented by the Activity or Fragment, with methods like showLoading() or showItems(list). The Presenter is a plain Kotlin class that holds the logic, has a reference to the View interface, and calls it imperatively. The contract is that pair of interfaces. It solved the testability problem: I can unit test the presenter on the JVM with a fake view. The cost is a manual attach/detach lifecycle and lots of boilerplate."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Passive view: the View has no logic; it only exposes setters and forwards events. The presenter pulls data, decides, and pushes results.

user click -> View.onClick -> presenter.onSaveClicked()
presenter -> repo.save() -> result
presenter -> view.showSaved()      (imperative push)

Because the presenter pushes into the view, state is spread across the view's current widget state and presenter fields. There is no single state object. The presenter also has a lifecycle problem: if it holds the view and an async result arrives after the view is detached, it either crashes or leaks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
interface LoginContract {
    interface View { fun showLoading(); fun showError(msg: String); fun navigateHome() }
    interface Presenter { fun attach(view: View); fun detach(); fun onLoginClicked(user: String, pass: String) }
}

class LoginPresenter(
    private val repo: AuthRepository,
    private val scope: CoroutineScope,
) : LoginContract.Presenter {
    private var view: LoginContract.View? = null
    private var job: Job? = null

    override fun attach(view: LoginContract.View) { this.view = view }
    override fun detach() { view = null; job?.cancel() }

    override fun onLoginClicked(user: String, pass: String) {
        view?.showLoading()
        job = scope.launch {
            repo.login(user, pass)
                .onSuccess { view?.navigateHome() }
                .onFailure { view?.showError(it.message.orEmpty()) }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting detach(), leaking the Activity via the presenter.
  • Putting Android types (Context, Intent) in the presenter, which kills JVM tests.
  • Presenter and view each keeping their own copy of state, so they diverge after recreation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Supervised vs passive view? → Passive: all logic in presenter. Supervising controller: view may do simple data binding itself.
  2. How do you keep the presenter across rotation? → Retained fragment, loaders, or a ViewModel hosting the presenter; none are automatic.
  3. Why is view?. null-safe calling a smell? → It hides dropped updates: if the view is gone, the update is silently lost and not replayed on reattach.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Presenter holds logic, view is an interface." Senior: points out the push model loses state across recreation, and that the attach/detach lifecycle is the core defect MVVM removes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams hit "view is null"/"Fragment not attached" crashes after backgrounding mid-request (see Q013).

questions.promptHtml: What is the real structural difference between MVP and MVVM on Android? Don't say "MVVM uses data binding".

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you can reason about dependency direction, not recite buzzwords.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The difference is who knows whom. In MVP the presenter has a reference to the view and pushes updates into it. In MVVM the ViewModel knows nothing about the view; it exposes observable state and the view subscribes. That reverses the dependency, so the ViewModel can outlive the view, survive rotation, and be reattached to a new view that simply collects the latest state. Data binding is one way to subscribe; collecting a StateFlow in Compose is another."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect MVP MVVM (Android)
Dependency Presenter -> View (interface) View -> ViewModel
Update style Imperative push (view.showX()) Observe state (pull on subscribe)
After view recreated Presenter must re-push everything New view reads current state
Lifecycle hooks Manual attach/detach None to the view; ViewModel scoped by owner
Android types Via View interface Should be none in ViewModel
Boilerplate Contract interfaces State type + observation

The key runtime consequence is "latest value replay": a StateFlow always has a current value, so a re-subscribing view gets consistent state. With a push-based presenter, anything pushed while detached is gone.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class LoginViewModel(private val repo: AuthRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(LoginUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<LoginUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun onLoginClicked(user: String, pass: String) {
        _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val r = repo.login(user, pass)
            _state.update { it.copy(loading = false, error = r.exceptionOrNull()?.message, loggedIn = r.isSuccess) }
        }
    }
}
data class LoginUiState(val loading: Boolean = false, val error: String? = null, val loggedIn: Boolean = false)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling any class suffixed ViewModel "MVVM" while it holds a View reference.
  • Exposing MutableStateFlow/MutableLiveData publicly.
  • Thinking MVVM implies two-way binding.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a ViewModel behave like a presenter? → Yes, if it calls a view interface; then you lose the lifecycle benefit and leak risk returns.
  2. Is MVVM on Android the same as Microsoft's MVVM? → Origins are similar (observable state, view binds), but Android's ViewModel class is primarily a lifecycle-scoped state holder.
  3. Where does MVVM struggle? → State can be scattered across many streams, allowing inconsistent combinations (the problem MVI's single state tackles, Q009).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists benefits. Senior: frames it as dependency inversion plus replayable state, and names the remaining weakness (state fragmentation).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Migrating MVP to MVVM typically deleted a whole class of "view detached" crashes, but introduced "state mutated from many places" bugs.

questions.promptHtml: Google says the ViewModel is a "screen-level state holder". How is that different from a presenter, and what should it not do?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who use ViewModel from people who understand its contract and limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A presenter drives the view. A ViewModel holds and produces UI state, and the UI decides how to render it. It's scoped by a ViewModelStoreOwner, so it survives configuration change and lives until the Activity finishes or the nav entry leaves the back stack. It should not reference views, Context or Resources, should not hold UI-behaviour logic like navigation calls, and doesn't survive process death by itself."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Per the official docs: ViewModel is a business-logic or screen-level state holder; it caches state through config changes; its lifetime equals the lifetime of its ViewModelStoreOwner (Activity until finish, navigation entry until removed from the back stack, or a composable owner when using the newer owner APIs, verify availability in your Lifecycle version). It cancels viewModelScope in onCleared().

Logic split from the events guide:

  • Business logic: what to do with state changes (payment, saving prefs). Data/domain layers and ViewModel.
  • UI behaviour logic: how to show state changes (navigation calls, showing a snackbar). The UI.

Docs also say not to use ViewModel as the holder for small reusable UI components (e.g. a chip group), because multiple instances under one owner share the same ViewModel unless you pass keys.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Wrong: UI behaviour and framework types in the ViewModel
class ProfileViewModel(private val ctx: Context, private val nav: NavController) : ViewModel() {
    fun onSaved() { Toast.makeText(ctx, "Saved", Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show(); nav.navigate("home") }
}

// Right: expose state, UI decides how to react
class ProfileViewModel(private val repo: ProfileRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(ProfileUiState())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()
    fun onSaveClicked(name: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        repo.save(name)
        _ui.update { it.copy(saved = true) }
    }
}
data class ProfileUiState(val saved: Boolean = false)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding an Activity/Context reference (leak, since the ViewModel outlives the Activity).
  • Assuming process death is covered.
  • One giant ViewModel for the whole app flow.
  • Passing the ViewModel itself into child composables rather than state plus lambdas.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Application context in a ViewModel? → Allowed via AndroidViewModel or injection, but prefer abstracting what you need (a string provider/resource interface).
  2. What survives process death? → Only what you put into SavedStateHandle or persist.
  3. Why not make everything a ViewModel? → Lifetimes are screen-scoped; small widgets get shared instances; plain state holder classes are cheaper (Q021).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel survives rotation." Senior: states the owner-scoped lifetime, the business vs UI-logic split, and the process-death gap.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Memory-leak reports with LeakCanary showing Activity retained by a ViewModel field are the classic symptom of Context in ViewModel.

questions.contextHtml:
A news app (1.2M DAU, 40% on devices with 3 GB RAM) crashes with 0.9% crash-free regression after a release. LeakCanary in debug shows MainActivity retained after rotation. Crash reports include IllegalStateException: Can't access the Fragment View's LifecycleOwner when getView() is null on a minority of sessions. This is the screen's code:

class FeedViewModel(
    private val activity: FeedActivity,            // "needed for string resources and dialogs"
    private val repo: FeedRepository,
) : ViewModel() {

    val feed = MutableLiveData<List<Article>>()

    init {
        repo.registerListener(object : FeedListener {      // singleton repo
            override fun onUpdated(list: List<Article>) {
                feed.value = list                          // called from a background thread
                activity.showUpdatedBanner()
            }
        })
    }

    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch { feed.value = repo.fetch() }
}
questions.promptHtml: Find every defect and tell me how you would restructure this.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Don't pass the activity." Stops there. Misses the listener leak, the main-thread violation and the exposed mutable state; no ownership of the listener's lifetime.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is registerListener threadsafe and what thread does it call back on? (affects setValue crash). Is the repo a singleton? (determines leak chain). Do we need the banner as a persistent thing or a one-shot? (state design). How is FeedViewModel created, a custom factory taking the activity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship a hotfix that removes the activity ctor param and replaces the banner with state, plus unregisters the listener in onCleared. If the release is the regression source, I'd stage the rollout back to 10% while the fix is built.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ViewModel holds the Activity, so every config change leaks one Activity (strongest, LeakCanary confirms). (b) Singleton repo holds the anonymous listener, which captures this (ViewModel) and thus the Activity, so the leak persists after the ViewModel is cleared. (c) feed.value = on a background thread throws IllegalStateException: Cannot invoke setValue on a background thread. (d) The Fragment-view exception is a red herring from another screen; verify via stack.
  4. How I'd verify each: LeakCanary leak trace (GC root: repo singleton -> listener -> ViewModel -> Activity). StrictMode/Looper assert on callback thread. Crash stack grouping in Crashlytics by screen. Unit test the ViewModel on the JVM; it won't compile once Activity is removed.
  5. Root cause: Lifetimes inverted: a longer-lived object (ViewModel, singleton) references a shorter-lived one (Activity), through a registration that is never undone. Plus thread confinement of LiveData violated.
  6. Fix: Short-term: drop Activity, add onCleared unregister, use postValue or collect on main. Long-term:
class FeedViewModel(private val repo: FeedRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(FeedUiState())
    val ui: StateFlow<FeedUiState> = _ui.asStateFlow()

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            repo.feedUpdates().collect { list ->               // cold Flow; unsubscribed on cancel
                _ui.update { it.copy(articles = list, showUpdatedBanner = true) }
            }
        }
    }
    fun refresh() = viewModelScope.launch { _ui.update { it.copy(articles = repo.fetch()) } }
    fun bannerShown() = _ui.update { it.copy(showUpdatedBanner = false) }
}
data class FeedUiState(val articles: List<Article> = emptyList(), val showUpdatedBanner: Boolean = false)

Strings resolved in the UI via stringResource; dialogs and banners are UI behaviour driven by state. 7. Prevention: LeakCanary in debug CI smoke test, lint/Konsist rule "ViewModel classes must not import android.app.Activity/Context/View", code-review checklist item for listener registrations (every register needs a visible unregister or a scoped Flow). 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not just switch to AndroidViewModel to "fix" it; that hides the Context problem and leaves the listener leak. I'd not use a WeakReference to the Activity; it masks the design flaw and makes banner behaviour nondeterministic.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the repo API is a callback and you can't change it? → Wrap in callbackFlow { ...; awaitClose { unregister } }.
  • How do you test it? → Fake repo emitting a MutableSharedFlow, assert ui after emission with runTest.
  • What if the banner must not re-show after rotation? → Clear it via bannerShown() once displayed; state, not a one-shot event (details in E1).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a team whose "temporary" Activity param in a ViewModel factory survived three refactors. After the leak was found, each rotation retained about 30 MB of bitmaps, and low-memory devices showed an elevated OOM rate until fixed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only "don't pass Activity".
  • Hire: finds Activity leak, singleton listener leak and background setValue; proposes Flow/state.
  • Strong hire: also gives the GC root chain, the lint enforcement, and refuses WeakReference/AndroidViewModel band-aids with reasons.

questions.promptHtml: What does Google's recommended Android architecture look like? Which layers are mandatory?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the shared vocabulary of every Android interview; vague answers signal shallow reading.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Google recommends at least two layers: a UI layer and a data layer, and an optional domain layer between them. The UI layer is UI elements plus state holders like ViewModel. The data layer is repositories, each with zero to many data sources, and holds the business logic and is the source of truth. The domain layer, use cases or interactors, is only added to encapsulate complex or reused logic. Data flows down as state, events flow up (UDF), and Google recommends Hilt for DI."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
events (clicks)  ^                    | state (immutable)
                         |                    v
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  | UI layer:   Compose/Views  <->  ViewModel (state) |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
                     |  (optional)
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  | Domain layer: use cases / interactors             |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
                     |
  +---------------------------------------------------+
  | Data layer: Repository -> data sources (net/db/file)|
  +---------------------------------------------------+

Points from the current guide: drive UI from persistent data models; assign a single source of truth per data type and expose it immutably; use UDF; types own their concurrency policy and are main-safe; reduce dependence on Android classes outside app components; expose as little as possible from each module. The guide itself says recommendations are "not mandatory" and should be adapted.

Note what is not in the guide: it never prescribes "MVVM" or "MVI" by name; it prescribes layers, state holders and UDF. People call it MVVM because ViewModel is the state holder.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ArticleRepository(
    private val remote: ArticleRemoteDataSource,
    private val local: ArticleDao,
) {
    val articles: Flow<List<Article>> = local.observeAll().map { rows -> rows.map { it.toDomain() } }
    suspend fun refresh() = local.upsert(remote.fetch().map { it.toEntity() })
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying the domain layer is required.
  • Thinking "MVVM" is the official name of the guidance.
  • Putting business logic in the ViewModel that belongs in the data layer.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When do you add the domain layer? → Complex logic, or logic reused by several ViewModels (Q018).
  2. Who owns the source of truth in offline-first apps? → Typically the database; the repository exposes it (A5/R1 detail).
  3. Does the guide require Clean Architecture? → No; it overlaps in layering but does not mandate the dependency-inversion boundaries or per-layer models.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: draws three boxes. Senior: states what is optional, what the guide deliberately leaves open, and which parts (SSOT, UDF, main-safety) carry the real value.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams that copied a three-layer diagram with pass-through use cases ended up with 300 files of boilerplate for 40 screens.

questions.promptHtml: What is MVI, and how do its parts map onto an Android screen?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: MVI is now a common team choice; you must explain it mechanically, not as "MVVM with a state class".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "MVI is a unidirectional loop: the View emits Intents (user actions), a pure function called a reducer takes the current state and a result and produces a new immutable State, and the View renders that single State. Side work like network calls runs outside the reducer and feeds results back as events. The properties I care about are one state object per screen, one entry point for changes, and a pure, unit-testable reducer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
View --Intent--> Processor/ViewModel --Result--> Reducer(state, result) --> new State
   ^                                                                           |
   +----------------------------- render(State) <-----------------------------+

Components:

  • State: one immutable data/sealed type for the entire screen.
  • Intent (user intention, not Android Intent): sealed class like LoadClicked, QueryChanged.
  • Reducer: (State, Result) -> State, no IO, no randomness, no clock; deterministic.
  • Side effects: network, DB happen in the processor, then reduce results. One-shot UI effects (navigation, snackbar) are a separate, debated channel (chunk E1).

Invariants this buys: any bug is reproducible from the sequence of intents, you can log/replay (time travel debugging in libraries like MVIKotlin), and impossible state combinations can be removed by modeling State as one type rather than several streams.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface SearchIntent {
    data class QueryChanged(val q: String) : SearchIntent
    data object Retry : SearchIntent
}

data class SearchState(val query: String = "", val loading: Boolean = false,
                       val results: List<String> = emptyList(), val error: String? = null)

private sealed interface Result {
    data class Query(val q: String) : Result
    data object Loading : Result
    data class Loaded(val items: List<String>) : Result
    data class Failed(val msg: String) : Result
}

private fun reduce(s: SearchState, r: Result): SearchState = when (r) {
    is Result.Query -> s.copy(query = r.q)
    Result.Loading -> s.copy(loading = true, error = null)
    is Result.Loaded -> s.copy(loading = false, results = r.items)
    is Result.Failed -> s.copy(loading = false, error = r.msg)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting IO in the reducer, making it impure and untestable.
  • Confusing MVI's "Intent" with android.content.Intent.
  • Mutable state collections inside the "immutable" State.
  • Treating one-shot effects as part of the pure loop without deciding semantics.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a reducer rather than state = state.copy(...) anywhere? → Single choke point for transitions; easier logging, testing, and race-safety.
  2. Is MVI the same as Redux? → Same unidirectional idea; Redux has a global store, Android MVI is typically per screen.
  3. Does MVI help with process death? → Not by itself; State must be serializable or rebuilt from persisted inputs (U1 covers this).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "MVI has a single state and intents." Senior: calls out the reducer purity guarantee, where side effects live, and the unresolved one-shot event question.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Time-travel/replay of recorded intents has been used to reproduce user-reported bugs from logged action sequences.

questions.promptHtml: Our team has MVVM with a StateFlow<UiState>. Another team uses MVI. What is actually different, and is the difference worth the boilerplate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The honest answer is nuanced; interviewers want judgment, not allegiance.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Good MVVM with one exposed StateFlow<UiState> and an update function is already most of MVI. What MVI adds is discipline: all input goes through a single onIntent(sealed) entry, state changes go through reducers, and the state is always one object. What you pay is boilerplate: an Intent class, Result class, and reducer per screen. I'd adopt strict MVI when screens have many interacting inputs or a team needs enforced consistency; for simple screens, MVVM with one state is enough."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dimension MVVM (state-flow flavour) MVI
Input Many public functions One onIntent(Intent) sealed entry
State One or several streams Exactly one State
Transitions _state.update { } anywhere Reducer only
Boilerplate Low Higher (Intent/Result/Reducer)
Debuggability Log per function Log one intent stream, replay
Risk Scattered updates, impossible combos Reducer growth, ceremony

Public sentiment in the community describes real-world code as "MVI-flavored MVVM": ViewModel with a single StateFlow and sealed event handler. Google's UDF guidance matches that shape without prescribing reducers.

Where MVVM breaks down in practice: several independent streams (isLoading, items, error as separate LiveData) allow states like loading=true, error="x" together, and the UI must combine them correctly. A single state type fixes that, in MVVM or MVI alike.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// MVVM style
fun onQueryChanged(q: String) { _state.update { it.copy(query = q) }; search(q) }
fun onRetry() = search(_state.value.query)

// MVI style: single entry
fun onIntent(i: SearchIntent) = when (i) {
    is SearchIntent.QueryChanged -> { reduce(Result.Query(i.q)); search(i.q) }
    SearchIntent.Retry -> search(_state.value.query)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Declaring one "better". Both are valid; context decides.
  • Assuming MVI removes concurrency bugs; races on async results still need care (Q016).
  • Intent classes that mirror methods 1:1 with no extra benefit.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a sealed Intent class cost runtime? → Negligible: one allocation per user action; the cost is code volume.
  2. Which is easier for new hires? → Public functions are more familiar; MVI has more concepts but clear rules.
  3. How do you share infrastructure to cut boilerplate? → A base Container/library (Orbit, MVIKotlin) or a small in-house reduce/onIntent helper.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: lists definitions. Senior: argues the real lever is single state plus enforced transitions, quantifies the boilerplate, and picks by screen complexity and team size.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An MVI migration was abandoned at a mid-size team after 60 screens because simple list screens gained 3 files each with no bug reduction; a hybrid (MVI only for complex forms) survived.

questions.contextHtml: You join a startup (6 Android engineers, 2 new hires per quarter). The app has 35 screens today and will reach about 80 in 18 months. Screens range from simple lists to a checkout and a chat screen with 7 concurrent inputs (typing, attachments, presence, retries, delivery receipts, network state, draft). The codebase mixes three styles. The CTO asks: "Pick one presentation architecture for everything and justify it in a meeting tomorrow."
questions.promptHtml: What do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "MVI because it's modern" or "MVVM because Google uses it." No team context, no migration cost, and one rigid rule for every screen.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the crash and bug distribution by screen? (shows where complexity hurts). Compose or Views today? How is test coverage on ViewModels? What is the new-hire ramp time target? Any KMP plans? (affects library choice).
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd freeze the style debate by writing a one-page decision record (ADR) with a default and an escape hatch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Most screens need only one StateFlow<UiState> plus function calls. (b) The chat screen justifies a reducer because inputs interact. (c) Inconsistency itself, not the pattern, is the main cost today. (d) Boilerplate fatigue will cause the strict approach to be skipped by deadline.
  4. How I'd verify each: Sample 10 recent bugs and tag root cause: state inconsistency vs missing test vs lifecycle. Count how many screens have more than 3 independent async inputs. Time a new engineer building one screen both ways in a spike.
  5. Root cause: The pain is inconsistent state modeling and no rules for transitions, not the absence of "MVI".
  6. Fix: Proposal: default is MVVM with a single immutable UiState exposed as StateFlow, one onEvent-style entry optional, state transitions via update. For screens that meet explicit criteria (3+ concurrent inputs or complex form with dependent fields), use a reducer-based variant with a pure reduce function and tests. Same State/UDF conventions everywhere so code reads the same.
  7. Prevention: Written criteria in the ADR; a ViewModel template in the repo; Konsist/lint checks for exposed mutable state and Context in ViewModels; review at 6 months with bug data.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not mandate strict MVI everywhere (boilerplate cost across 80 screens; 6 engineers means the tax is felt every sprint). I would not allow three patterns indefinitely either (onboarding cost). I would not bring a framework before we know the home-grown helper is insufficient.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The CTO insists on one pattern, no exceptions. → Then choose MVVM with single UiState plus optional reducer helper inside it, since it is a superset and degrades gracefully.
  • Half the team wants Orbit. → Fine for the complex screens if it meets KMP/testing needs; evaluate maintenance and version (Orbit docs show 12.x); isolate behind our own base class.
  • What if we go KMP later? → Keep ViewModels free of Android types; state/reducers are then shareable.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team spent a quarter converting everything to strict MVI, then found that bug counts didn't change; the real reduction came from deleting four separate isLoading flags in just the three worst screens.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: names a pattern, no reasoning.
  • Hire: ties choice to screen complexity and team size, proposes a default with criteria.
  • Strong hire: gathers data first, writes an ADR, proposes enforcement, and states the cost of both extremes.

questions.promptHtml: How does testability differ across MVC, MVP, MVVM and MVI, and what actually makes presentation code easy to test?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Testable" is the most-claimed benefit and rarely explained.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Testability comes from seams, not from the pattern name: can I run the logic on the JVM, replace dependencies, and assert on outputs? MVC fails because logic sits in the Activity. MVP passes if the presenter has no Android types, using a fake view and verifying calls, which is brittle because tests assert interactions. MVVM and MVI let me assert on state: given inputs, what is the latest state. MVI is the easiest because the reducer is a pure function and state is a single object."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
What I assert changes with the pattern:

  • MVP: interaction-based: "was showError() called once after showLoading()?" Tests couple to the view interface; order mistakes cause failures.
  • MVVM/MVI: state-based: collect uiState, assert a sequence of states or the final one. Refactoring internals does not break tests.
  • MVI reducer: reduce(state, result) == expected, no coroutines, no mocks.

Requirements for JVM testing: ViewModel has no Android types; dispatchers injected (or Dispatchers.setMain(StandardTestDispatcher())); repositories as interfaces with fakes; time controlled by runTest virtual time.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
class SearchViewModelTest {
    @get:Rule val main = MainDispatcherRule() // sets Dispatchers.Main to a test dispatcher

    @Test fun `query emits loading then results`() = runTest {
        val vm = SearchViewModel(FakeSearchRepo(listOf("kotlin")))
        vm.onQueryChanged("kot")
        advanceUntilIdle()
        assertEquals(listOf("kotlin"), vm.state.value.results)
        assertFalse(vm.state.value.loading)
    }
}

@Test fun `reducer sets error`() {
    val s = reduce(SearchState(loading = true), Result.Failed("x"))
    assertEquals(SearchState(loading = false, error = "x"), s)
}

(MainDispatcherRule is a small test rule you write once, as in Google's samples.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using Dispatchers.Main in tests without setMain (crashes: "Module with the Main dispatcher had failed to initialize").
  • Asserting only the final state with StateFlow conflation and missing intermediate states.
  • Over-mocking with Mockito instead of fakes, which re-couples tests to implementation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. StateFlow conflation and tests? → Rapid updates can be skipped; use Turbine (test {}) with an unconfined collector, or assert the final state when intermediates don't matter.
  2. Fake vs mock? → Fakes keep behavior; mocks verify interactions; prefer fakes for repositories.
  3. Where do you still need UI tests? → Rendering, accessibility, navigation wiring; ViewModel tests do not cover them.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "MVVM is more testable." Senior: explains state-based vs interaction-based assertions, the seams needed, and the coroutine test setup.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team with Mockito-verify MVP tests saw 400 tests break during a harmless refactor and then deleted them, leaving coverage at zero for the module.

questions.promptHtml: Compare how MVP and MVVM/MVI handle rotation, backgrounding and process death. What happens to in-flight work and state in each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is where "I used it" separates from "I understand what it does at runtime".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Rotation: an MVP presenter lives with the view unless I retain it myself; a ViewModel survives by default and keeps running coroutines. Backgrounding: neither stops work automatically; I choose collection policy (lifecycle-aware collection) to avoid wasted rendering. Process death: both lose everything in memory. ViewModel plus SavedStateHandle can restore small keys like IDs and query; anything big must be rebuilt from persistence. The pattern doesn't give process-death safety; what I persist does."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeline for an Activity with a ViewModel:

onCreate #1 -> ViewModel created, request fired
rotate -> Activity destroyed, ViewModel kept, request continues
onCreate #2 -> same ViewModel, collect latest state
back pressed / finish -> ViewModel.onCleared() -> viewModelScope cancelled
OS kills process in background -> all memory gone; on return Activity recreated, ViewModel NEW

MVP without retention: presenter recreated with the Activity, so the request restarts or the result is dropped. Retaining via a retained Fragment or a ViewModel hosting it gives config-change survival but the presenter-to-view reference must be cleared on detach.

Backgrounding: a ViewModel keeps its scope alive while the owner exists. If the UI collects with plain collect in lifecycleScope.launch, it keeps collecting while stopped; use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle() (Lifecycle 2.6+). stateIn(WhileSubscribed(5_000)) lets upstream stop 5 s after the last subscriber leaves, surviving a rotation (which gap is typically shorter than 5 s) while still stopping when truly backgrounded.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class DetailViewModel(
    private val savedState: SavedStateHandle,
    private val repo: ItemRepository,
) : ViewModel() {
    private val id: String = checkNotNull(savedState["id"]) // survives process death via the Bundle
    val ui: StateFlow<DetailUiState> = repo.observe(id)
        .map { DetailUiState.Success(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), DetailUiState.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Stuffing large lists in SavedStateHandle (Bundle limit ~1 MB shared across the whole transaction; TransactionTooLargeException).
  • Assuming a ViewModel's in-flight request survives process death.
  • Collecting in onStart with launch and never cancelling, duplicating collectors on each start.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I test process death? → Developer options "Don't keep activities" for activity destruction; adb shell am kill <pkg> while backgrounded for true process death.
  2. Why 5 seconds in WhileSubscribed? → Covers config-change gap and brief app switches; value is a convention from Google guidance, tune with data.
  3. Where should a draft that must survive process death live? → In SavedStateHandle if small, otherwise Room/DataStore, written as the user types with debounce.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "ViewModel survives rotation." Senior: gives the three-lifetime model (config change, backgrounding, process death), what each pattern does, and the verification technique.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Blank screen after returning from background" reports from low-RAM devices were process death with a ViewModel that held the only copy of an ID in memory.

questions.contextHtml:
A fintech app (800k DAU, mostly mid-range Android 11-14 devices) is on MVP with Fragments. After a release that added a 6-second "download statements" call, crash-free sessions drop from 99.6% to 98.4% (about 1.2 points). Top crash, 61% of the regression:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Fragment StatementsFragment{...} not attached to an activity.
  at androidx.fragment.app.Fragment.requireContext(Fragment.java:...)
  at com.app.statements.StatementsFragment.showDownloaded(StatementsFragment.kt:88)
  at com.app.statements.StatementsPresenter$onDownloadClicked$1.invokeSuspend(StatementsPresenter.kt:54)

It correlates with users who tap download, then switch apps or rotate. A second, smaller crash is an NPE in the presenter, view!!. Backend p95 for the call rose from 1.5 s to 6 s the same week (red herring for cause, but it widened the window).
questions.promptHtml: Walk me through diagnosis, fix, and what you would change structurally.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add if (isAdded) checks everywhere." Treats symptoms, leaves lost results, and keeps the lifecycle coupling.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the crash exist before at low rate? (the slow backend widens a latent bug). Is the presenter retained across rotation? Is the coroutine scope tied to the presenter or to the Fragment? Should a completed download still be delivered if the user left the screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: in detach() cancel the job and null the view; in the callback use view?. instead of !!; stage rollout. Optionally, server-side cap the call to reduce the window while the client fix goes out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Presenter coroutine outlives the Fragment and calls into a detached view (stack trace says this). (b) view!! after detach() sets it to null. (c) Backend slowness only lengthened the window; (d) a new library version changed dispatch (unlikely; the stack shows our code).
  4. How I'd verify each: Crashlytics breadcrumbs for lifecycle events; reproduce with a debug proxy delaying the response 8 s then rotate/background; check Job ownership in code; confirm the crash rate by app version and by backend latency bucket.
  5. Root cause: Push-based presenter with a manual attach/detach contract: the async result is delivered to a view that is no longer valid. The lifecycle is enforced by convention rather than by structure.
  6. Fix: Short-term as above. Long-term, make the result state, not a call: the download outcome is held in a state holder and rendered when a view exists.
class StatementsViewModel(private val repo: StatementsRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(StatementsUiState())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()

    fun onDownloadClicked() {
        if (_ui.value.downloading) return                       // idempotent
        _ui.update { it.copy(downloading = true) }
        viewModelScope.launch {
            val r = repo.download()
            _ui.update { it.copy(downloading = false, downloadedFile = r.getOrNull(), error = r.exceptionOrNull()?.message) }
        }
    }
}
data class StatementsUiState(val downloading: Boolean = false, val downloadedFile: Uri? = null, val error: String? = null)

If the user must be notified even after leaving the screen, use WorkManager (A5) plus a notification, not a screen-bound scope. 7. Prevention: Crash-free alert at 0.3 points per release in staged rollout; a UI test that rotates mid-request; lint rule banning !! on view references; code-review item "who cancels this job". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not wrap every call in isAdded (the update is silently lost). I would not do a big-bang MVVM migration in the hotfix (see Q019 for the incremental path). I would not just make the backend faster and call it fixed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the download must finish even if the user closes the app? → That is background work: WorkManager with a foreground service for long jobs, observable status.
  • What if rotation re-triggers onDownloadClicked? → Guard on state (downloading) and make the call idempotent via a request id.
  • Can you keep MVP and make this safe? → Yes: presenter scope cancelled in detach, a cached last state replayed on attach; but you are re-implementing a ViewModel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found the real fix cost less than the hotfix debate: moving the single worst screen to a state holder removed 70% of that crash class, which justified the broader migration budget.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: isAdded checks only.
  • Hire: cancels job on detach, reproduces with delayed response and rotation, proposes state-based delivery.
  • Strong hire: separates screen-bound from background work, makes the request idempotent, and sets rollout/alert guardrails.

questions.promptHtml: Why must an MVI reducer be pure, and what goes wrong when it is not? Where do side effects live instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand the guarantee MVI provides and can enforce it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A reducer is (State, Result) -> State. Pure means no IO, no clock, no randomness, no reading mutable fields. Then given the same sequence of results I always get the same states, so I can unit test with plain assertions, replay a bug, and log transitions. If I put a network call or System.currentTimeMillis() inside, tests become flaky, replay breaks, and state transitions can race. Side effects live in the processor/ViewModel layer, which dispatches results to the reducer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Properties lost when impure:

  1. Determinism: replay of logged intents no longer reproduces the screen.
  2. Thread safety: a pure function over immutable data needs no locks; if the reducer reads this.cache, concurrent calls race.
  3. Testing: no coroutine scaffolding is needed.

Where effects go:

Intent -> [Processor: suspend, IO, timers] -> Result -> [Reducer: pure] -> State

Time is injected: pass now inside the Result (Result.Tick(nowMillis)), not read in the reducer. IDs: generate in the processor and carry in the Result.

The scheduling of the reducer matters too: if multiple coroutines call it concurrently, the read-modify-write on the state holder must be atomic (MutableStateFlow.update uses compare-and-set and retries the lambda, which is another reason the lambda must be pure and cheap; it may run more than once).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: impure reducer
fun reduce(s: CartState, r: CartResult): CartState = when (r) {
    is CartResult.Added -> s.copy(
        items = s.items + r.item,
        updatedAt = System.currentTimeMillis(),   // hidden input: clock
        id = UUID.randomUUID().toString(),        // hidden input: randomness
    )
    else -> s
}

// Correct: inputs travel in the result
data class Added(val item: Item, val now: Long, val id: String) : CartResult
// reducer: s.copy(items = s.items + r.item, updatedAt = r.now, id = r.id)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Side effects inside update {}: the lambda may be retried under contention, so it would run twice.
  • Mutating a list inside the state (items.add) and re-emitting the same reference; StateFlow equality check sees no change and the UI does not update.
  • A reducer that depends on previous Intents held in ViewModel fields rather than in State.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does StateFlow.update retry the lambda? → It uses compare-and-set on the value; on conflict it recomputes from the new value.
  2. Where does validation go? → Either in the processor (reject before a Result) or as a pure state derivation in the reducer; not as IO.
  3. How do you test ordering races? → Fire intents from multiple coroutines in runTest with a test dispatcher and assert invariants (totals), not an exact sequence.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Reducer returns a new state." Senior: lists the hidden-input categories, explains CAS retries, and where each effect belongs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An order total that differed between server and device was traced to a reducer reading the device clock for a promo-expiry check, making the bug unreproducible from logs.

questions.promptHtml: You have heard of Orbit and MVIKotlin. When would you use an MVI library on Android instead of a hand-rolled ViewModel, and what are the risks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Build-vs-buy judgment for architecture infrastructure.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Libraries give you a standard container for state and effects, plus test tooling, so the team doesn't invent its own base class. Orbit is a lightweight Kotlin Multiplatform MVI framework: a ViewModel hosts a container, logic runs in intent {} blocks, state changes via reduce {}, one-shots via postSideEffect. MVIKotlin is heavier and more strict: a Store with executor and reducer, no coroutine dependency in core, plus logging and time-travel debugging. I'd pick one when several teams need consistency or KMP sharing; I'd avoid it when a 30-line base class does the job, because a library is a long-term dependency in every screen."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the project pages: Orbit's docs show a ViewModel implementing a container host with an initial state, with intent {}, reduce {} and postSideEffect(...), and require state and side effect types to be comparable and recommend immutable; artifacts are published for core, viewmodel, compose and test (docs showed 12.x at time of reading; verify). MVIKotlin describes itself as an extendable KMP MVI framework with logging and time travel, with Reaktive and coroutines extensions as separate modules (check Maven Central for the latest version).

Trade-offs:

Concern Hand-rolled Library
Consistency Needs conventions Enforced by API
Learning curve Low Medium (DSL, concepts)
Test tooling Write your own Provided (e.g. Orbit test module)
Lock-in None Every screen depends on it
Bus factor Your team Maintainer(s)
KMP Own work Both claim KMP support

Mitigation: wrap the library behind your own thin base class (or interface) so a swap touches one file, and review the library's release cadence and issue activity before adopting.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Orbit-style (per its docs; check current API for your version)
class CounterViewModel : ViewModel(), ContainerHost<CounterState, CounterEffect> {
    override val container = container<CounterState, CounterEffect>(CounterState())

    fun add(n: Int) = intent {
        reduce { state.copy(total = state.total + n) }
        if (state.total > 100) postSideEffect(CounterEffect.Limit)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Adopting a library to fix an inconsistency that is really a missing convention.
  • Letting library types leak into UI and domain modules.
  • Using side effects for state that should survive rotation.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reduce lock-in? → Own interface in a core module with a library-backed implementation; UI only sees StateFlow.
  2. What is the downside of postSideEffect? → It is the one-shot channel debate (E1); delivery guarantees depend on collector presence.
  3. Why might MVIKotlin suit KMP? → Core has no dependency on a reactive library and targets many platforms.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: names libraries. Senior: states what each gives and costs, mentions KMP and wrapping strategy, and defaults to the smallest thing that works.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that adopted a niche MVI library saw upstream development slow; a wrapper interface let them migrate 90 screens module by module instead of at once.

questions.contextHtml:
A search screen on an e-commerce app (3M MAU, p95 search latency 900 ms on 4G) uses MVI-style code. QA reports "results sometimes show for the previous query" at about 2% of sessions, and sometimes the spinner never stops. Logs:

D/Search: intent QueryChanged("sh")   t=0
D/Search: intent QueryChanged("shoe") t=250
D/Search: result Loaded("shoe") t=700
D/Search: result Loaded("sh")   t=1100   <- state shows results for "sh", query field says "shoe"

Code:

class SearchViewModel(private val repo: SearchRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SearchState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    fun onIntent(i: SearchIntent) {
        if (i is SearchIntent.QueryChanged) {
            _state.value = _state.value.copy(query = i.q, loading = true)
            viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
                val items = repo.search(i.q)                         // 200-1500 ms
                _state.value = _state.value.copy(results = items, loading = false)
            }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, and how do you fix it properly?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a debounce." Reduces frequency but does not fix ordering or the lost update; also misses the non-atomic value = value.copy.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is repo.search cancellable? Should typing cancel previous requests? Is there a minimum query length? Any caching by query?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Track a searchJob and cancel it on each new query, with a guard so a late result can't apply to a different query.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Out-of-order responses: older request finishes after the newer one and overwrites (log proves it). (b) Lost update: _state.value = _state.value.copy(...) is read-modify-write across threads (Default dispatcher), so a concurrent write is overwritten, causing a stuck spinner. (c) Server-side ordering/cache is a red herring; the client must be robust anyway.
  4. How I'd verify each: Log with request ids; a runTest with a fake repo whose delays are inverted (first call slower) and assert the final state; stress test with concurrent writes to see lost updates.
  5. Root cause: Two bugs: no cancellation or sequencing of async work (stale result wins), and non-atomic state updates from multiple threads.
  6. Fix: Cancel the previous job and update atomically; better, model it as a flow with collectLatest/mapLatest.
class SearchViewModel(private val repo: SearchRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val queries = MutableStateFlow("")
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SearchState())
    val state = _state.asStateFlow()

    init {
        viewModelScope.launch {
            queries.debounce(250).distinctUntilChanged()
                .collectLatest { q ->                              // cancels in-flight search
                    _state.update { it.copy(loading = true) }
                    val items = runCatching { repo.search(q) }.getOrDefault(emptyList())
                    _state.update { it.copy(results = items, loading = false) }
                }
        }
    }
    fun onIntent(i: SearchIntent) {
        if (i is SearchIntent.QueryChanged) {
            _state.update { it.copy(query = i.q) }                 // echo immediately
            queries.value = i.q
        }
    }
}

(Real code should map errors to an error state rather than getOrDefault, and rethrow CancellationException; runCatching swallows it, so use try/catch that rethrows. Flow cancellation details are in the coroutines track.) 7. Prevention: A test with reversed latencies for every screen that fires async work from user input; a review rule "no value = value.copy, use update"; detekt/Konsist rule for it. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not rely on Dispatchers.Default for state writes at all (the work can be there, writes use update). I would not use a global mutex serializing all searches; it adds latency instead of cancelling stale work. I would not trust server ordering.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the API isn't cancellable? → Cancel at the coroutine level so the result is dropped; the HTTP call may finish, so use OkHttp call cancellation via suspendCancellableCoroutine (Retrofit suspend functions cancel the call).
  • Why was the spinner stuck? → Write A (loading=true) was overwritten by B's loading=false copy from an older snapshot, or vice versa.
  • Does debounce 250 ms change p95? → It adds 250 ms to every search; trade-off against request volume.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite incident: one stale result overwrote another and showed a different user's item in a shared-device kiosk; a state-tagging request id and collectLatest fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests debounce only.
  • Hire: identifies stale overwrite and non-atomic update; uses cancel/collectLatest and update.
  • Strong hire: writes the reversed-latency test, discusses cancellation semantics and error handling, and sets lint enforcement.

questions.promptHtml: In MVI the View sends sealed Intent objects; in MVVM it calls ViewModel functions. Is that difference meaningful, especially with Compose?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes whether you can separate real architectural value from ceremony.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Mechanically a sealed Intent is a reified function call. The value is a single serializable entry point: I can log, queue, replay, interceptors, and exhaustively when over it. The cost is mapping every UI event to a class and passing a (Intent) -> Unit down the tree. In Compose, passing one onIntent lambda reduces parameter lists, but it makes previews and child composables depend on the whole Intent vocabulary and hurts skippability if the lambda isn't remembered or stable. I'd use Intents for complex screens and plain functions elsewhere."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Reified calls give you:

  • Exhaustive handling via sealed when; adding an intent forces a compile error at the handler.
  • A single choke point for analytics, logging, debouncing or middleware.
  • Possible serialization for replay.

They cost you:

  • Boilerplate per action.
  • Coupling: a leaf composable that takes (ProfileIntent) -> Unit knows every intent, while a leaf with onFollowClicked: () -> Unit knows one.
  • Compose stability: lambdas capturing unstable values may defeat skipping; with Strong Skipping Mode (default from Kotlin 2.0.20 compiler plugin; verify for your version) lambdas are memoized automatically, which reduces but does not remove the concern. Compose details are in the A3 track.

Guidance I use: hoist events as specific lambdas at leaf level, and map them to Intents at the screen-level composable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
@Composable
fun ProfileRoute(vm: ProfileViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    ProfileScreen(
        state = state,
        onFollowClick = { vm.onIntent(ProfileIntent.Follow) },   // map at the boundary
        onNameChange = { vm.onIntent(ProfileIntent.NameChanged(it)) },
    )
}

@Composable
fun ProfileScreen(state: ProfileState, onFollowClick: () -> Unit, onNameChange: (String) -> Unit) { /* ... */ }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Passing vm or onIntent into every leaf composable.
  • Creating Intent subclasses for purely local UI state (expand/collapse) that never needed the ViewModel.
  • Using data class Intents with large payloads for high-frequency events (text input), allocating per keystroke needlessly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Local UI state: Intent or remember? → remember; only business-relevant events go to the ViewModel (official events guidance).
  2. Can you debounce at the intent level? → Yes, a flow of intents with debounce for specific types; clearer than ad-hoc jobs.
  3. How do intents help analytics? → One interceptor logs all events with consistent naming instead of sprinkling calls.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "Intents are cleaner." Senior: lists what the reification actually buys, the Compose coupling cost, and the boundary-mapping pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that passed onIntent into 40 composables saw preview files require full fake intent handlers; refactoring to leaf lambdas cut preview boilerplate by roughly half.

questions.promptHtml: Where does business logic live in your presentation architecture: Presenter, ViewModel, use case or repository? How do you stop the ViewModel becoming a god class?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common real failure of MVVM is the 2,000-line ViewModel.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "I split logic by kind. Data rules that exist regardless of the screen (merging sources, caching, conflict resolution) belong in the data layer. Logic reused by several screens or genuinely complex goes into a domain-layer use case. Screen state production and mapping domain data into UI state belongs in the ViewModel. UI behaviour like navigation and animations stays in the UI. If a ViewModel grows past a few hundred lines, I extract by responsibility: a use case, a mapper, or a plain state-holder class for a sub-feature."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Placement table:

Logic Home Why
Fetch + cache + merge Repository Single source of truth, reuse
Rule reused by 2+ ViewModels, or complex Use case (optional domain) Avoid duplication
Combine flows into UiState, formatting for the screen ViewModel (or mapper it calls) Screen-specific
Navigation, snackbars, focus, animation UI / UI state holder UI behaviour logic

Google's guide describes the domain layer as optional, "use it only when needed". The smell test for a use case: if it only calls one repository method and returns the result, it adds a file and nothing else. The test for a needed one: it combines multiple repositories, enforces a rule, or is reused.

God-ViewModel symptoms: constructor with 10+ dependencies, multiple unrelated StateFlows, tests needing a 40-line setup. Decompose by extracting use cases for logic, mapper functions for UiState building, and sub-state-holders (plain classes taking a CoroutineScope) for independent sections of a screen.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ObserveCartSummaryUseCase(
    private val cart: CartRepository,
    private val promos: PromoRepository,
) {
    operator fun invoke(): Flow<CartSummary> =
        combine(cart.items, promos.active) { items, promo -> CartSummary.from(items, promo) }
}

class CartViewModel(observeSummary: ObserveCartSummaryUseCase) : ViewModel() {
    val ui: StateFlow<CartUiState> = observeSummary()
        .map { CartUiState.Content(it.toUi()) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), CartUiState.Loading)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Use case per repository method (pass-through boilerplate).
  • UI formatting (colors, strings) in the domain layer.
  • The ViewModel doing database transactions or JSON parsing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many dependencies is too many? → No hard number; more than about 6 distinct collaborators means multiple responsibilities.
  2. Use case with invoke operator vs named method? → Style; invoke reads well for single-action classes; consistency matters more.
  3. How do you refactor a god-ViewModel safely? → Characterization tests first, extract one responsibility at a time behind the same public state (the Chunk X scenarios go deeper).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "business logic goes in the ViewModel (or use cases)." Senior: classifies logic types, applies a smell test for use cases, and gives a decomposition path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Merge conflicts concentrated in one ViewModel file across three teams were the trigger to extract use cases and sub-state holders.

questions.contextHtml: A travel app with 2.5M DAU has 120 screens on MVP (Java + Kotlin mix), a 4.2-star rating, and 1.1% of sessions crashing. Leadership wants "MVVM with Compose" in 9 months, with no feature freeze, a release every 2 weeks, 8 Android engineers, and a hard requirement that conversion funnel metrics may not drop. Roughly 15 screens (search, booking, payment) generate 70% of revenue.
questions.promptHtml: How do you plan and execute the migration?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite screen by screen, start at the top of the list." No risk ordering, no safety nets, no definition of done, nothing about coexistence.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the test coverage on presenters? What are the top crash screens (data, not guesses)? What is the quality bar for the revenue flows? Are there feature teams that own screens? Is Java still being written?
  2. Immediate mitigation: No mitigation needed as such; the first action is a safety net: crash and funnel dashboards per screen and a staged-rollout policy (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) with abort thresholds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The riskiest part is not the architecture but regression in revenue flows. (b) Coexistence cost (two patterns) will be paid for 9 months, so interfaces between old and new must be thin. (c) Presenter logic is entangled with views. (d) Team capacity: 8 engineers can't convert 120 screens plus features.
  4. How I'd verify each: Funnel-event coverage audit; presenter test coverage report; count of screens by size and change frequency from git history (churn drives value); spike converting one medium screen to measure real cost per screen.
  5. Root cause: N/A (planning problem); the underlying driver is lifecycle-crash classes and slow onboarding.
  6. Fix (plan): Strangler approach:
    • Extract logic first, UI later: new ViewModel exposing state, with the old Fragment rendering it (view-layer unchanged). This captures lifecycle benefits at lower risk.
    • Wrap an MVP presenter's output in a state adapter where needed:
// Interim: ViewModel hosts the legacy presenter's logic through a state adapter
class LegacyBridgeViewModel(private val repo: BookingRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _ui = MutableStateFlow(BookingUiState())
    val ui = _ui.asStateFlow()
    fun onSearch(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch { _ui.update { it.copy(results = repo.search(q)) } }
}
  • Order: (1) top-crash screens, (2) high-churn screens, (3) revenue-critical flows last and behind a flag with parallel-run comparison (new vs old results logged), (4) long tail opportunistically when touched ("boy scout" rule).
  • Compose adoption via ComposeView inside existing Fragments, decoupled from the ViewModel migration.
  • Definition of done per screen: presenter deleted, ViewModel unit tests, no regression on screen funnel metric across a full week.
  1. Prevention: Lint/Konsist rule: no new presenters; a scoreboard of screens migrated; a template and sample so engineers don't invent styles.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not freeze features (business won't accept; 9 months). I would not migrate payment first (highest risk, least learning). I would not promise 100% of 120 screens in 9 months; I'd commit to the top 40 by crash and churn and a policy for the rest.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• A migrated screen regresses conversion by 2%. → Roll back via flag, compare event streams old vs new, diff behaviour (often debounce or double-fire differences).
  • Capacity halves mid-project. → Cut scope by data (stop at churn threshold), keep the no-new-presenter rule.
  • Two teams want different MVVM styles. → One ADR, one template; enforce through review and checks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team shipped ViewModel-hosting with the old Fragments first; crash rate on those screens dropped within one release, which earned the trust to continue, while the Compose rewrite followed at its own pace.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "rewrite all screens".
  • Hire: strangler, ordered by risk and value, staged rollouts.
  • Strong hire: separates logic migration from UI migration, uses parallel-run/flags on critical flows, defines done and scope-cut rules.

questions.contextHtml: An internal-tools startup app (3 engineers, 14 screens: login, lists, detail, forms; 50k DAU, no offline mode) is being started from scratch. A candidate engineer on your team proposes: "Clean Architecture, strict MVI, 14 feature modules, a domain layer with use cases, mappers between 4 model types." Another says "just MVVM, one module." The product manager says "we need the first version in 8 weeks and then it'll grow, I don't know how much."
questions.promptHtml: What do you decide, and how do you reason about it when the future is unknown?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Chooses the fancier architecture "because it will scale", or the simplest "because YAGNI" without any trigger for revisiting.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "grow" mean: more screens, more engineers, new platforms? What is the data complexity (single backend, caching needs)? Is there any known compliance/testing requirement? What is the hiring plan?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I'd avoid irreversible decisions and keep seams cheap to add later.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) With 3 engineers the dominant risk is delivery speed, not coordination. (b) The costs of 14 modules plus 4 model types (build config, mapping code) outweigh benefit at this size. (c) The cheapest valuable investments are single UiState, state holders without Android types, repository interfaces, and DI. (d) Later splitting is possible if package boundaries are clean.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype one feature vertically and count files and time; check build time on the baseline; list trigger events that justify the next step (e.g., more than 6 engineers, build over 5 minutes, a second app).
  5. Root cause: N/A; the real question is the cost of being wrong in each direction. Over-building is a certain cost now; under-building is a possible cost later that is lower if seams exist.
  6. Fix (decision): Single app module with package-by-feature, MVVM with one immutable UiState per screen, repositories behind interfaces, Hilt, unit-tested ViewModels. Use a domain layer only where logic is reused. Use DTO-to-UI mapping only where shapes differ. Write an ADR with explicit triggers: introduce modules when build exceeds a threshold or team exceeds N; introduce a reducer for screens with 3+ concurrent inputs.
com.app.feature.orders/   OrdersScreen, OrdersViewModel, OrdersUiState
com.app.data.orders/      OrdersRepository (interface + impl), OrdersApi
com.app.core.ui/          shared components
  1. Prevention: Konsist or architecture test enforcing "feature packages don't import each other's internals"; this keeps a later module split mechanical.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build the maximal architecture upfront (premature abstraction slows 3 people by perhaps 20-30% by my estimate, verify with the spike). I would not skip tests and DI either, because that is expensive to retrofit. I would not hide the decision: the ADR makes revisiting cheap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The CEO wants an iOS app next year. → Keep ViewModel/data logic Kotlin-only and free of Android types so KMP sharing is feasible (Z1 chunk), but don't create the KMP module until it's committed.
  • A senior hire insists on MVI. → Allow a reducer on the complex screens; consistent State and UDF conventions stay the same.
  • Build time becomes 6 minutes at month 10. → That is the ADR trigger to modularize by the existing package boundaries.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite 4-person team built 11 modules in month one, then spent most of month three untangling a cyclic dependency while the competitor shipped; a later team with package boundaries split into modules in two days.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks by fashion.
  • Hire: matches architecture to team size and screen complexity, keeps seams.
  • Strong hire: defines explicit triggers, writes it down, quantifies cost, and protects reversibility.

questions.contextHtml: You are building a reusable DateRangePicker component used in 5 screens, some of them in tablet layouts showing two pickers side by side (departure and return). A teammate wrote DateRangeViewModel and calls hiltViewModel() inside the component. QA finds that on the tablet screen both pickers show the same selection, and when the user selects in one, the other changes. A reviewer asks: "do reusable components even need ViewModels?"
questions.promptHtml: Why is this happening, and what should the component's state design be?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Give the ViewModels different keys" as the only answer, without questioning whether a ViewModel is the right tool.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the picker contain business logic (availability from a backend) or only UI selection logic? Does the selection need to survive process death? Who owns the selected value, the picker or the screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Quick patch: supply a distinct key per usage (hiltViewModel(key = "departure")), which unblocks QA.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Both composables resolve the same ViewModel instance because they are under the same ViewModelStoreOwner (the nav entry) and use the same default key. (b) A shared singleton holding state (less likely, check). (c) Recomposition issue (red herring, since the symptom is shared value).
  4. How I'd verify each: Log System.identityHashCode(vm) in both usages; check owner via LocalViewModelStoreOwner; reproduce with two pickers in a preview/test.
  5. Root cause: A ViewModel's identity is (owner, key, class). Two usages under one owner without keys share one instance. The official docs warn against ViewModels as state holders for reusable components for exactly this reason.
  6. Fix: Make the picker stateless plus a small plain state holder; the screen's ViewModel owns the selected values.
@Stable
class DateRangePickerState(initial: DateRange? = null) {
    var range by mutableStateOf(initial)
        private set
    fun select(r: DateRange) { range = r }
    companion object {
        val Saver: Saver<DateRangePickerState, *> = Saver(
