            save = { it.range?.let { r -> listOf(r.startEpochDay, r.endEpochDay) } },
            restore = { DateRangePickerState(DateRange(it[0], it[1])) },
        )
    }
}

@Composable
fun rememberDateRangePickerState(initial: DateRange? = null) =
    rememberSaveable(saver = DateRangePickerState.Saver) { DateRangePickerState(initial) }

@Composable
fun DateRangePicker(state: DateRangePickerState, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) { /* UI only */ }

For screens needing the value in business logic, hoist: the screen ViewModel keeps departure and return in UiState, and the picker is controlled (range, onRangeChange). 7. Prevention: Guideline: "ViewModels are for screens; reusable components take state and callbacks or a plain state holder"; a code review check for hiltViewModel() inside ui/components. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not keep key-per-usage as the permanent design: callers must remember keys, and the component can't be previewed or tested without DI. I would not use a global singleton to share state.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The picker needs backend availability data. → Pass availability as parameters from the screen ViewModel; the component stays dumb.
  • Should the plain state holder survive configuration change? → rememberSaveable with a Saver handles config change and process death for small data.
  • Where do plain state holders fit officially? → Docs separate business-logic state holders (ViewModel) from UI-element state holders (plain classes) (A3 covers remember/rememberSaveable mechanics).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite design-system team had 9 components each with its own ViewModel; moving to state holders removed DI from their preview catalog and cut preview setup code significantly.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only adds keys.
  • Hire: explains ViewModel identity and shared owner, proposes hoisting/state holder.
  • Strong hire: separates UI-element state from business state, mentions Saver/process death, and sets a team guideline.

questions.contextHtml: A trading-style watchlist screen was built with MVI single state: one WatchlistState data class with 38 fields (prices list of 50 rows, selected tab, filters, banner, sort order, connection status...). It worked at launch with prices updating once per 5 s. Product now wants live prices at up to 10 updates/s per row for 50 visible rows (so up to 500 tick events/s), on a device mix where 35% are low-end (2 GB RAM, 6-core budget CPUs). Beta shows jank: p95 frame time 38 ms (budget is 16.7 ms at 60 Hz), 11% janky frames, and battery complaints. Layout Inspector shows every row recomposing when any one price changes.
questions.promptHtml: What do you change, in architecture terms, before touching micro-optimizations?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use remember and derivedStateOf in the rows" with no change to how state is produced or shaped, or "MVI doesn't scale, go back to MVVM".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does every tick need to reach the UI (can we sample at 100-250 ms)? Are all 50 rows visible at once, or does a list virtualize? What fields change at high frequency vs rarely? Is the tick source a WebSocket with coalescing possible?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Sample/conflate ticks to a UI cadence (e.g. one batched update per 250 ms, about 4 updates/s regardless of tick rate) and ship behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) One big state with an unstable list: every tick creates a new state and a new list, and rows depending on it recompose. (b) 500 emissions/s each allocating a 50-element list copy. (c) Per-row work (formatting numbers, color calc) done in composition. (d) Heavy recompositions caused by unstable parameters (a List is treated as unstable without immutable collections or a compiler config; Compose stability details in A3). (e) Slow network layer is a red herring; the profile shows UI thread.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts; Perfetto/System trace and JankStats for frame timing; Compose compiler reports for stability; allocation profiler for list copies; Macrobenchmark scroll/update test comparing before and after.
  5. Root cause: Granularity mismatch: a slow-changing screen state and a high-frequency per-row stream share one value, so the highest-frequency change defines the update rate of everything. Math: 500 events/s x 50-row copy = 25,000 row objects/s allocated, plus recomposition checks of every row on each state change.
  6. Fix: Split state by change rate and scope:
    • Screen state (tab, filters, banner): StateFlow<WatchlistUiState> updated rarely.
    • Row prices: a per-instrument stream or Map<Id, Price> snapshot exposed separately, batched.
class WatchlistViewModel(private val prices: PriceRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _screen = MutableStateFlow(WatchlistScreenState())
    val screen = _screen.asStateFlow()                              // rarely changes

    val priceTicks: StateFlow<Map<String, Price>> = prices.ticks()  // Flow<Tick>
        .chunkedByTime(250)                                          // custom operator: batch within 250 ms
        .scan(emptyMap<String, Price>()) { acc, batch -> acc + batch.associate { it.id to it.price } }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyMap())
}

(chunkedByTime is not a stdlib operator; implement with a ticker/conflate or use sample(250) if dropping intermediate ticks is acceptable.) In the UI, rows take a single Price by id and use stable keys; read the price in the lowest scope (or via a lambda () -> Price) so only affected rows recompose. 7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark with jank threshold in CI; a rule: state containing streams with different change rates gets split; Compose compiler stability reports reviewed on UI-layer PRs. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not abandon single-state wholesale: the screen state benefits remain; the fix is scoping, not dropping UDF. I would not sample if correctness requires every tick (then batch, don't drop). Two streams reintroduce the possibility of inconsistent combinations, so keep them independent concerns, not coupled values.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compliance says every tick must be recorded. → Record at the repository (all ticks), but UI consumes sampled output.
  • 4K tablets show 200 rows. → Virtualized list (LazyColumn with keys) only composes visible rows; verify visible count.
  • Battery drain persists. → Stop collecting when the screen isn't visible (lifecycle-aware collection plus WhileSubscribed), reduce socket subscriptions to visible symbols.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team cut recompositions on a live-price screen by roughly an order of magnitude only after splitting state by change rate; earlier attempts at remember tweaks showed no measurable gain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: micro-optimizations or blames MVI.
  • Hire: splits state by rate, batches/samples ticks, uses profiling tools.
  • Strong hire: quantifies allocation and event rates, preserves UDF benefits, and builds benchmark guardrails.
